options.text: Instruct the network contractor to begin installing the cabling at once under its existing order, and bring the cost through change control once the work is under way.
options.rationale: The candidate is right about the urgency but commits €140,000 of unapproved work. Starting first and seeking approval afterwards turns change control into a record of decisions already made.

options.text: Ask the insurer's legal team to challenge the landlord's reading of the lease formally, and hold the cabling question open until that dispute has been settled.
options.rationale: The legal team has already confirmed the landlord's position. The candidate spends the seven weeks on a dispute the client does not expect to win, while the floor-closure date approaches.

options.text: Treat the cabling as outside the project, add it to the scope statement's exclusions, and tell the insurer's facilities team that it must arrange the work separately.
options.rationale: An office without data cabling is not a usable office, so excluding it hides a dependency rather than resolving it. Deciding the boundary unilaterally also takes a scope decision away from the sponsor.

questions.explanation: Assumptions in a scope statement are part of what the baseline rests on, so when one is shown to be false the scope has to be re-examined rather than defended. The response is to accept the new fact, size its effect on scope, cost and schedule, and put the resulting change to whoever approves the baseline, early enough for the decision still to matter. Acting before approval, contesting a settled fact or quietly moving the work outside the boundary each avoids that decision instead of enabling it.
questions.mindset: When an assumption fails, take the new fact as given and re-plan through the baseline, quickly.

questions.stem: Three days into a two-week sprint, a payroll software company's team is building support for a proposed change to employee tax allowances; it is the entire sprint goal. The government announces that the change has been withdrawn and will not happen. About a third of the sprint's work is done, and the product backlog holds plenty of other valuable items. Which two actions best fit agile practice?

options.text: The product owner decides whether to cancel the sprint, since its goal no longer has any value to the business.
options.rationale: When a sprint goal becomes obsolete, cancelling the sprint is an option, and the decision belongs to the product owner because it is a judgement about value.

options.text: The team finishes the sprint as planned, because the sprint backlog was committed and changing it mid-sprint breaks the timebox.
options.rationale: The timebox protects a goal, and this goal no longer exists. The candidate is honouring the form of the commitment after its purpose has gone, spending ten days on work nobody will use.

options.text: The project manager cancels the sprint straight away, because the announcement has made its goal impossible to achieve.
options.rationale: The reasoning about the goal is right, but cancelling a sprint is the product owner's call. The candidate is acting on the correct conclusion without the authority to do so.

options.text: If the sprint is cancelled, the team holds a new sprint planning with a fresh goal drawn from the reordered product backlog.
options.rationale: Cancellation is followed by planning a new sprint, so the team's capacity goes straight to the next most valuable work with a coherent goal rather than a loose collection of items.

options.text: The team keeps the sprint running and swaps in backlog items of equal size, so that velocity and the sprint length are both preserved.
options.rationale: Swapping items keeps the team busy but leaves a sprint with no goal to guide trade-offs. The candidate protects the metrics and the calendar rather than the coherence of the work.

options.text: The team completes the tax-allowance stories already started, so the effort spent so far is not wasted, then picks up new items.
options.rationale: Finishing work whose purpose has disappeared adds cost without adding value. The candidate is letting effort already spent justify spending more.

questions.explanation: A sprint's scope exists to serve its goal, so when the goal becomes obsolete the scope has no reason to stand. The response is to let the person accountable for value decide whether to stop, and then re-plan around the next most valuable goal. Finishing obsolete work, preserving metrics or acting on someone else's authority all put the mechanics of the sprint ahead of the reason it exists.
questions.mindset: When the goal goes, let the plan go with it.

questions.stem: A music festival is commissioning a new ticketing website under a fixed-price contract. Reviewing the requirements document before it is baselined, you find 64 functional requirements covering browsing, basket, payment and e-tickets, but nothing about how many buyers the site must handle at release time, how quickly pages must load or what availability is expected. Last year, 40,000 people queued in the first ten minutes of the general sale. Which two actions should the project manager take before the baseline is agreed?

options.text: Work with the festival's ticketing and operations leads to define measurable capacity, response-time and availability requirements, using last year's release-day demand as the basis.
options.rationale: Performance expectations exist whether or not anyone wrote them down. Turning them into measurable requirements now puts them in the fixed price instead of leaving them to be argued about on sale day.

options.text: Add each new performance requirement to the requirements traceability matrix with a linked test, so that the supplier's testing has to show every one of them being met.
options.rationale: A requirement with no verification attached can be agreed and then never demonstrated. Tracing each to a test makes the supplier prove the site meets the release-day load before it is accepted.

options.text: Rely on the hosting service level that the tender already asks each bidder to state, rather than adding requirements that the festival's organisers have not themselves raised.
options.rationale: A hosting service level covers whether the servers are up, not whether the site copes with 40,000 buyers at once. The candidate mistakes the organisers' silence for an absence of need.

options.text: Ask the supplier to size the platform generously for peak demand and to include the extra hosting cost as a provisional sum within its fixed-price bid.
options.rationale: Generously sized is not a target anyone can test against. The candidate hands the definition of adequate to the party paid to deliver it, and the provisional sum reopens the price it was meant to fix.

options.text: Baseline the functional requirements on schedule and plan a load test shortly before go-live, to find out how much demand the finished site can actually handle.
options.rationale: A load test without a stated target has no pass mark, and running it just before go-live finds the gap when the design can no longer change cheaply. The candidate treats measurement as a substitute for a requirement.

questions.explanation: Requirements documentation is incomplete until the qualities a solution must have are stated alongside what it must do. Capacity, speed, availability and similar qualities are usually assumed by stakeholders rather than voiced, so the project manager has to draw them out, express them as measurable thresholds and attach a means of verification to each. Under a fixed price this matters doubly, because anything unstated is something the supplier was never paid to deliver.
questions.mindset: Treat what stakeholders take for granted as requirements that still need writing down.

questions.stem: On a court service's case-management replacement, the business analyst must decide how to elicit requirements from three different groups. Match each situation to the elicitation technique that suits it best. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Listing clerks book hearings so quickly and habitually that, when interviewed, they cannot describe the steps they actually follow.
Around 900 magistrates across forty courts must be asked which of twelve candidate features matter most to them, within three weeks.
Listing, finance and judicial office leads each own part of the end-to-end process and disagree about where one stage ends and the next begins.

options.text: Observation of the work as it is done
options.rationale: When expertise has become habit, people describe what they think they do rather than what they do. Watching the work captures the steps, shortcuts and workarounds an interview would miss.

options.text: Questionnaire
options.rationale: A large, dispersed group answering a bounded question in a short time is the case questionnaires are built for. Interviews or workshops could not reach 900 people in three weeks.

options.text: Facilitated cross-functional workshop
options.rationale: The disagreement is about hand-offs between groups, so it can only be resolved with all of them in the room. A facilitator helps them agree the boundaries together rather than separately.

options.text: Benchmarking against another organisation's system
options.rationale: Not used. Benchmarking shows what others do and can inspire options, but none of these situations lacks ideas: each lacks access to what the service's own people know or need.

questions.explanation: Elicitation technique follows the nature of the gap in knowledge. Tacit, habitual knowledge needs observation; a large population with a bounded question needs a questionnaire; disagreement across group boundaries needs those groups together under facilitation. Choosing by what is familiar, rather than by what kind of knowledge is missing, produces confident requirements that are incomplete.
questions.mindset: Choose how to ask by working out what kind of knowledge is missing.

questions.stem: A streaming service's product owner uses different prioritisation techniques for different backlog questions. Match each situation to the technique that answers it best. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Items vary widely in size, and some lose value quickly: a licensing feature is worthless if it misses a rights deadline in eight weeks.
The team needs to know which features subscribers take for granted, so that their absence causes anger, and which would genuinely delight them.
A launch date is fixed, and stakeholders must agree which items the release cannot ship without and which can drop if time runs out.

options.text: Weighted shortest job first (cost of delay divided by duration)
options.rationale: When value decays at different rates and sizes differ, ordering by cost of delay over duration puts urgent, small items first and stops large, slow-decaying items blocking them.

options.text: Kano analysis
options.rationale: Kano classifies features by how their presence or absence affects satisfaction, separating basic expectations from delighters, which is exactly the question being asked.

options.text: MoSCoW (must, should, could, won't)
options.rationale: With time fixed, scope is the variable, and MoSCoW makes stakeholders draw the line between what the release must contain and what can fall away under time pressure.

options.text: 100-point method (stakeholders divide 100 points across items)
options.rationale: Not used. It captures the relative preference of a group of stakeholders, but none of these questions turns on preference: they turn on time sensitivity, customer perception and a must-have line.

questions.explanation: Prioritisation techniques answer different questions, so the choice starts with the question. Time-sensitive value against varying size calls for cost of delay; how features affect customer satisfaction calls for a satisfaction model; a fixed date calls for a clear line between essential and droppable scope. Using one technique for every question gives tidy orderings that answer the wrong thing.
questions.mindset: Pick the prioritisation technique by the question you need answered.

questions.stem: A parcel carrier's programme builds a depot extension under a predictive contract and a driver app in two-week sprints. Complete each sentence with where the scope item should be held. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The steering committee funds the capability 'drivers capture proof of delivery in the app', with a budget and a target quarter. It belongs in
A driver suggests that proof of delivery should let them photograph where a parcel was left. It belongs in
Installing the extension's loading-bay doors to the agreed specification, with its own cost and acceptance criteria. It belongs in

options.text: the approved release plan as a funded feature, held at that level by the committee
options.rationale: The committee governs capability, budget and timing, so the feature sits at the level it approves. The detail of how drivers capture proof is left to the team's backlog beneath it.

options.text: the product backlog, for the product owner to refine and order
options.rationale: A suggestion about how a feature should work is a candidate story. The product owner weighs it against everything else; it changes no approved baseline and needs no committee decision.

options.text: a work package in the WBS, described in the WBS dictionary
options.rationale: Fully specified physical work with its own cost and acceptance criteria is exactly what a predictive work package holds, and the dictionary carries the detail the contractor builds to.

options.text: the current sprint backlog, for the team to start straight away
options.rationale: Not used. Nothing here is urgent or already part of the sprint goal, and adding items mid-sprint bypasses the product owner's ordering. Even the driver's idea goes to the product backlog first.

questions.explanation: A hybrid programme holds scope at different levels in different artefacts, and putting each item at the right level is what keeps governance light and detail flexible. Funded capability belongs at the level the governing body approves; detail of how that capability works belongs in the product backlog; fully specified predictive work belongs in work packages. Pushing detail upwards clogs governance, and pushing commitments downwards hides them.
questions.mindset: Hold each piece of scope at the level of the person who decides it.

questions.stem: A fitness app team has six sprints left before a fixed launch date. Its last eight sprints delivered between 34 and 42 points each, and the product owner forecasts with the lowest and highest of these. The ordered release backlog holds 290 points. Work out the forecast range and the scope at risk.

blanks.label: Points the team can expect to complete at its lowest velocity
blanks.rationale: Six sprints at the lowest observed velocity: 6 × 34 = 204 points. Items down to this point in the ordered backlog are the ones the release can reasonably commit to.

blanks.label: Points the team might complete at its highest velocity
blanks.rationale: Six sprints at the highest observed velocity: 6 × 42 = 252 points. Items between 204 and 252 points may make the release if the team performs at the top of its range.

blanks.label: Points of ordered backlog beyond even the highest forecast
blanks.rationale: 290 − 252 = 38 points. This scope is unlikely to ship by the launch date and should be presented to stakeholders as a trade-off decision now, not discovered in the final sprint.

questions.explanation: With a fixed date, a velocity range turns an ordered backlog into three bands: what will very likely ship, what might, and what almost certainly will not. Forecasting with a range rather than an average makes the uncertainty visible, and drawing the bands on the ordered backlog shows stakeholders exactly which items sit in each. The lower band is the commitment; the upper band is the trade-off conversation to have early.
questions.mindset: Forecast a fixed date as a range, and show which scope falls in each part of it.

questions.stem: The context diagram for a café chain's new loyalty system shows five external interfaces. Each label states how the draft scope statement treats that interface. Before the scope baseline is approved, select the interface that still needs a scope decision.

graphic.title: Context diagram of a loyalty system with five external interfaces and their scope status
graphic.caption: Select an interface. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between interfaces, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Till system: sends each purchase to the loyalty system. In scope; data specification agreed
regions.rationale: Listed as in scope with an agreed specification, so its boundary is settled. It is the most prominent interface, which is why it draws attention, but nothing about it is undecided.

regions.label: Card payment provider: no data exchanged. Listed under exclusions
regions.rationale: An explicit exclusion is a scope decision, not a gap. Candidates sometimes pick it because it involves no work, but the scope statement has already said so.

regions.label: Marketing agency: receives a monthly customer extract. Shown on the diagram only; in neither inclusions nor exclusions
regions.rationale: The diagram shows a data flow that the scope statement neither includes nor excludes, so nobody has decided whether building it is part of the project. That is exactly the kind of gap that becomes a dispute after baselining.

regions.label: Mobile app stores: host the customer app. In scope; publishing listed as a deliverable
regions.rationale: Publishing is named as a deliverable, so the interface is inside the boundary and accounted for. Its external ownership does not make its scope unclear.

regions.label: Head-office finance: receives a points-liability report. In scope; report format agreed
regions.rationale: Both the inclusion and the report format are agreed, so this interface needs no further decision before the baseline is approved.

questions.explanation: A context diagram is a check on the scope statement: every interface it shows should be either included, with enough definition to build, or explicitly excluded. An interface that appears on the diagram but in neither list is an undecided boundary, and undecided boundaries are where scope disputes start. Reconcile the two documents before baselining, so each external flow has a recorded decision.
questions.mindset: Every line crossing the boundary needs a recorded decision on which side it falls.
